0.0.n: Refers to a nonworking day, which may be a weekend or holiday.

0.1.n: Links 休日 to 朝ご飯, specifying when the meal is eaten.

0.2.n: Combines with ご飯 to make 朝ご飯, the everyday word for breakfast.

0.3.n: ご飯 can mean rice or a meal; here it forms part of 朝ご飯.

0.4.n: Links 朝ご飯 to 定番, identifying the meal these usual choices belong to.

0.5.n: Describes an established, familiar choice rather than something unusual.

0.6.n: Marks 定番 as the topic: the sentence explains what the usual choices are.

0.8.n: This borrowed food word is written in katakana.

0.9.n: Lists examples without suggesting they are the only choices.

0.10.n: Japanese nouns do not distinguish singular from plural, so this can refer to one or several.

0.11.n: Politely ends the statement identifying the usual breakfast choices.

1.0.n: Refers to a nonworking day, not necessarily Saturday or Sunday.

1.1.n: Links 休日 to 午前中, specifying which mornings are being discussed.

1.2.n: Refers to the period before noon, rather than just early morning.

1.3.n: Makes mornings on days off the time setting for the statement.

1.5.n: A noun naming the activity that is the purpose of going out.

1.6.n: Marks 買い物 as the purpose of going, rather than a destination.

1.7.n: The plain form of 行く comes before こと to turn the action into a noun-like phrase.

1.8.n: Turns 行く into something that can be described as frequent.

1.9.n: Marks the whole action 買い物に行くこと as what occurs frequently.

1.10.n: 多い means numerous; after an action plus ことが, it expresses frequency, and です adds politeness.

0.lit: As for day-off breakfast staples, they are pizza, pancakes, and the like.
0.tip: や introduces examples, so pizza and pancakes are not presented as the only breakfast choices.

1.lit: As for mornings on days off, occasions of going shopping are many.
1.tip: A plain verb plus ことが多いです means the action happens often; the person doing it is left unstated.
